Use the marked arc and the positions of $A$ and $B$ to decide whether to increase or decrease the angle of $A$.

Which ordered pair gives the Cartesian coordinates of $B$?

Both points lie on the same circle, so $B$ has radius $3$. Along the marked arc, moving from $A$ to $B$ is clockwise; subtract the marked angle.

$$
\theta_B=240^\circ-30^\circ=210^\circ.
$$

Thus $B$ has polar coordinates $(3,210^\circ)$. Using $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
x &=3\cos\left(210^\circ\right)=3\left(- \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)=- \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2},\\y &=3\sin\left(210^\circ\right)=3\left(- \frac{1}{2}\right)=- \frac{3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The Cartesian coordinates of $B$ are $(- \frac{3 \sqrt{3}}{2},- \frac{3}{2})$.

$$
n=\frac{a(t)\,i+b(t)\,j}{||{r}^{′}(t)||}.
$$

Find the function $a(t).$
question.:question/worked-solution:
For convenience, we express $r(t)$ in column vector notation:

$$
r(t)=\begin{bmatrix}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}
$$

To calculate the outward-pointing normal vector of a closed, positively oriented curve, we follow three steps:

**Step 1**: We compute the tangent vector ${r}^{′}(t).$

Differentiating the expression for $r(t),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\begin{bmatrix}{x}^{′}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Since $C$ is oriented counterclockwise, we rotate ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ *clockwise* to obtain an outward-pointing normal vector.

The rotation matrix that corresponds to a ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise rotation is

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}.
$$

Rotating the vector ${r}^{′}(t)$ by ${90}^{∘}$ clockwise, we get

$$
\begin{bmatrix}0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\ 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}4\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\ 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\end{bmatrix}.
$$

**Step 3**: Finally, we normalize the vector found in step 2.

Note that the magnitude of the vector found in step 2 equals the magnitude of ${r}^{′}(t)$ (since they differ only by a rotation). Therefore,

$$

$$

Finally, we conclude that $a(t)=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t.$

The area of the triangle $△ABC$ is $\frac{121\sqrt{3}}{18}\,\text{cm}^{2}.$ Find $AC.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The formula for the area of the triangle is 

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}bc\operatorname{sin}⁡A,
$$

where $∠A$ is between the sides of lengths $b$ and $c.$ 

Here

$$
\begin{aligned}c & =AB=\frac{22}{3}\text{ cm} \\ b & =AC \\ m∠A & ={120}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since 

$$
\operatorname{sin}⁡{120}^{∘}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2},
$$

we can calculate $b=AC,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot c\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡A \\ \frac{121\sqrt{3}}{18} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot \frac{22}{3}\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡{120}^{∘} \\ \frac{121\sqrt{3}}{18} & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot b\cdot \frac{22}{3}\cdot \left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) \\ \frac{121\sqrt{3}}{18} & =\frac{11\sqrt{3}}{6}b \\ b & =\frac{\frac{121\sqrt{3}}{18}}{\frac{11\sqrt{3}}{6}} \\ b & =\frac{11}{3}\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that $AC=\frac{11}{3}\,\text{cm}.$
